title: Clarity That Sticks
tagline: Clarity as a two-way skill: ask, restate, and close the loop in writing.
description: A 45-minute virtual session for all Vanderbilt staff: ask for clear expectations, restate them in your own words, and close the loop in writing so agreements survive the week.
heroLead: Two people often leave one conversation carrying different versions of it, and the rework lands weeks later. This session teaches the three moves that prevent it.
objectives: Ask the three clarity questions before accepting any significant task
Restate an expectation in your own words and surface the gaps early
Close the loop in writing the same day so the agreement survives
missionTie: A university out to define the century loses more hours to fuzzy expectations than to hard problems, and every clean handoff is Exceptional Core Operations in miniature.

agenda.d: Three questions that turn a vague request into a real expectation.
Restating in your own words, and judging when a handoff is clear enough to act on.
The same-day written line that makes an agreement survive the week.

manifesto: Write the agreement down the same day: what you heard, what you own, by when.

sections.headline: Ask the three clarity questions.
sections.lead: Requests like make it better sound clear and leave everything open. Before accepting significant work, get three answers: what does done look like, when is it needed, who decides? Gallup ranks knowing what is expected of you as the most basic employee need.
sections.group: In pairs: name a current task where you could not describe what done looks like. What would you ask, and of whom? 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Name one current task where you cannot describe what done looks like. Write the clarity question you will ask, and to whom.

deeper.title: When the requester does not know yet
deeper.body: Sometimes the honest answer to what does done look like is: I do not know yet. That answer is useful too. It tells you the task is exploratory, so agree on a checkpoint instead of a deliverable: I will bring a rough version Thursday and we will look at it together. And when the asker is senior, bundle the three questions into one sentence that reads as momentum: so I aim this right, what does done look like and by when?
steps: Write the bundled one-sentence version of the three questions in your own voice, one you could say to the most senior person you work with.
Pick one live task with no picture of done. Decide whether it needs the three questions or a checkpoint agreement, then send the ask today.

card.text: Before accepting any significant task, get answers to three things: what does done look like, when is it actually needed, and who makes the final call? Asking them is a service to the requester; every one you skip becomes a guess you own.

interaction.context: Requests like make it better feel clear while everyone is nodding. Gallup's Q12 engagement survey opens with the most basic employee need, I know what is expected of me at work, because nothing else engages until that does. The three clarity questions are how you claim it on any task, from anyone.
interaction.discuss: Think of a task that went sideways on you this year. Which of the three answers was missing at the start, and what stopped anyone from asking?
interaction.q: Quick check: asking your manager what done looks like is...

opts.t: Risky; it could read as pushback
opts.why: Vagueness is the risky option; you inherit every wrong guess. A clarity question early costs seconds and reads as ownership.
Exactly. The requester usually discovers their own picture is fuzzy while answering. You just saved the rework.

opts.t: Only worth it on big projects
opts.why: Small fuzzy tasks pile up into the same rework as big ones. The questions take ten seconds; make them a reflex.

sections.headline: The restate finds gaps while they are cheap.
sections.lead: Restating an expectation in your own words is the cheapest test it will ever get. A match buys you confidence, and a mismatch finds the gap while fixing it still costs minutes. The judgment call is knowing which handoffs need it.
sections.group: Breakout pairs: name a live handoff in your work that nobody has said back yet. What would your restate be? 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Name a live handoff nobody has said back yet. Write your one-sentence restate of it.

deeper.title: Restating up, down, and sideways
deeper.body: The restate flexes with the relationship. With a peer it can be casual: so I take the data pull and you take the writeup, right? With someone senior, attach it to your next step so it reads as motion: I will start with the survey data, since done means the summary by Friday. And when a handoff has more than three moving parts, restate in writing; a short list is easier to correct than a paragraph of talk.
steps: Take the live handoff from your solo prompt and write two restates: the casual peer version and the one you would send someone senior.
Use one of them in the real conversation this week. Whatever correction comes back is rework you just saved.

interaction.intro: For each handoff, check for done, deadline, and decider, then call it: act, say it back, or close in writing. Misjudging this is where rework starts.
labels: Agreed, close the loop in writing
interaction.passMsg: You can hear the difference. Clear gets action, fuzzy gets a restate, and every verbal agreement gets a written shadow.
interaction.failMsg: Close. The tell: look for done, deadline, and decider. Missing any of them, say it back. Agreed out loud only, write it down.

items.q: A colleague asks you to tighten up the proposal before it goes to the dean's office next month.
items.why: Tighten up could mean trim the wording or rebuild the budget section. Say back your version of done and let them correct it while it is cheap.

items.q: Your manager asks for the three enrollment charts, in the shared deck, by Thursday at noon.
items.why: Done, deadline, and destination are all named. Restating a fully clear request can read as stalling; this one you just do.

items.q: In a hallway chat, you and a peer split a project: you take the data pull, they take the writeup.
items.why: Verbal splits evaporate by Friday. One same-day message naming who owns what turns a nice chat into an agreement.

sections.headline: Agreements survive in writing.
sections.lead: The last move happens after the conversation: a short written line, same day, saying what you heard and what happens next. Ninety seconds of typing is the difference between an agreement and a memory. Build the close you would actually send.

deeper.title: Anatomy of a close that settles arguments
deeper.body: A working close reads like this: Thanks for the planning talk. What I heard: full draft to you by the 15th, I own the data section, you own the intro. Flag anything I got off. Notice the last line. The close is a test, and the best result is a correction within the hour, because that reply just saved you the rework. Silence becomes agreement you can point to; a correction is a gap caught while it costs nothing.
steps: Build your reusable three-line close in your notes app: what I heard, what I own, by when, plus the flag-anything line at the end.
Send one real close today for the most recent agreement you made, even if the conversation was days ago. One late close still beats none.

interaction.intro: You just left a planning conversation with real commitments in it. Choose how you restate and how you close the loop; the choices decide whether the agreement still exists in two weeks.

slots.key: How you restate in the room

opts.t: Got it, sounds good, will do.
opts.coach: Agreement noises test nothing. You can nod along to an expectation you heard completely differently, and people often do.

opts.t: Repeat their exact words back to them.
opts.coach: Parroting proves you listened. Your own words prove you understood, and that is the version that exposes a gap.

opts.t: So done means the draft to you by Friday, and I own the data section. Missing anything?
opts.coach: Own words, specifics, and an invitation to correct. This is the restate that finds the gap while fixing it is free.

opts.t: No follow-up; the conversation was clear enough.
opts.coach: Even a perfect conversation fades. In two weeks you will both trust your memories, and your memories will disagree.

opts.t: A recap message sometime next week, when things calm down.
opts.coach: Right move, late clock. By next week you are writing what you remember instead of what was said, and the two drift apart fast.

opts.t: A three-line message the same day: what I heard, what I own, by when.
opts.coach: Same day, short, and checkable. Anyone who misread the meeting now has a cheap moment to say so, in writing.

heads.strong: An agreement with a paper trail. Everyone can point at the same words all month.
heads.mid: A good conversation with a slow echo. Most of it survived; the fuzzy edges did not.
heads.weak: A warm memory. Two people are now working from two different meetings.

reactions.strong: Two weeks later a scope question pops up and gets settled in one minute by scrolling to your message. The project never even noticed the wobble.
reactions.mid: Your late recap mostly matched their memory. The one line that did not is the deliverable currently being built twice.
reactions.weak: The deadline arrives and so does the surprise: they expected the full draft, you finished the data section. The chat was pleasant; the rework is real.

recap.q: Before accepting a significant task, you should know...
recap.why: Those three answers turn a request into an expectation. Every one you skip becomes a guess you own later.

opts: A quick yes to keep things moving
Your own words, plus an invitation to correct
recap.why: Your own words test understanding, and the invitation makes correcting you cheap. Gaps found now cost minutes.

recap.q: A verbal agreement becomes durable when...
opts: You write it down the same day
Your manager was in the room
recap.why: Same-day writing captures what was said instead of what got remembered. Ninety seconds now beats an argument later.

recapMsgs.high: You have the three moves. Use them on one real expectation this week.
recapMsgs.mid: Solid. Revisit the section you missed, then build your clarity card.
recapMsgs.low: Worth a second pass through the three moves before you pick your expectation.

capstone.headline: One fuzzy expectation, made solid.
capstone.lead: Pick a real expectation in your week that would fail the done test. Roles only, never names; nothing you type is saved or sent.
capstone.whoLabel: Which expectation, and with whom? Roles only.
capstone.whoPlaceholder: e.g. the dashboard refresh; my manager and the ops lead
capstone.practiceLabel: Which move does it need first?

practices.name: The clarity ask
practices.move: Ask the three questions out loud: what does done look like, when is it actually needed, who decides?

practices.name: The say-back
practices.move: Restate the expectation in your own words and end with: am I missing anything?

practices.name: The written close
practices.move: Send a three-line same-day message: what I heard, what I own, by when.

whens.out: The move happens today, while the expectation is still cheap to fix.
The move opens your next conversation about that work, first thing.
Done by Friday, before the fuzzy version does any damage.

capstone.evidenceRow: Afterward, one line: what gap did the restate or the written close surface?

closing.headline: Ask, restate, and put it in writing.
closing.lead: Use the ask, the say-back, and the written close on one real expectation this week. That wraps the manager standard week.
closing.nextTag: Your one next step · This week
closing.nextBody: Ask, restate, or close the loop on the expectation you named. Notice what the move surfaces; that gap was headed for your calendar anyway.
closing.brandline: Ask. Say it back. Write it down.

facilitator.audience: All Vanderbilt staff in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm; nobody is assumed to manage anyone. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. No prerequisites; pairs naturally with this week's Monday and Tuesday sessions.
facilitator.pulse: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Did you run the move on your clarity card? What gap did it surface? Which of the three moves is becoming a reflex?' Count of completed clarity moves is the month's practice signal.

s1.title: The clarity ask
s1.purpose: Install the three clarity questions as a reflex before accepting significant work.
s1.say: Think of the last task that went sideways on you. Odds are it was never clear to begin with: make it better, own this going forward. Those requests feel clear for about an hour. Gallup has measured engagement with the same twelve questions for decades, and the first one is simply, I know what is expected of me at work. Everything downstream depends on it. Three questions get you there, and anyone can ask them of anyone: what does done look like, when is it actually needed, and who makes the call?
facilitate: Read the concept card once; let it sit.
Walk the In the room context; name the three answers slowly. No quiz in the live room.
Open the discussion prompt on the sideways task; take two or three voices.
Run the breakout on the task with no picture of done.

ask.q: What makes people swallow the clarity questions instead of asking them?
expect: Assuming it will become clear later
ask.respond: All real. Here is the reframe: the requester usually has a fuzzy picture too, and your question does them a favor. Later never clarifies anything on its own.

s1.debrief: Done, deadline, decider. Three answers turn a request into an expectation; skipped, they turn into guesses you own.
s1.watchFor: People treating this as manager-only material. Keep the framing two-way: peers hand each other fuzzy work constantly.
s1.transition: Asking is half the skill. The other half is proving you heard it right.
s1.coreNote: Core: skip the breakout; ask for one fuzzy task in chat instead.

s2.title: Say it back
s2.purpose: Train the restate: judging when an expectation is clear enough to act on and testing it in your own words.
s2.say: The restate is the cheapest quality check in working life. You say the expectation back in your own words and end with: am I missing anything? Ninety percent of the time you get a nod and free confidence. The other ten percent you find a gap while it still costs minutes instead of weeks. Let's train the judgment call.
facilitate: Run Clear enough? live; everyone plays on their own screen.
Pause after the hallway-agreement round; that one splits the room usefully.
Run the breakout on the handoff nobody has said back.

ask.q: Why can restating a fully clear request backfire?
ask.respond: Right, so the skill includes knowing when to just start. Restate when done, deadline, or decider is missing; act when all three are on the table.

s2.debrief: When done, the deadline, or the decider is missing, say it back in your own words. When all three are on the table, just start.
s2.watchFor: Word-for-word parroting in the examples. Push for own words: parroting proves listening, restating proves understanding.
s2.transition: One move left: making the agreement survive the week.
s2.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, take one voice on the debrief question.

s3.title: Close the loop
s3.purpose: Make the same-day written close a habit: what I heard, what I own, by when.
s3.say: Every agreement has a half-life. The conversation was perfect, everyone nodded, and two weeks later there are two honest, different memories of it. The written close stops the decay: three lines, same day. What I heard, what I own, by when. Ninety seconds of typing that replaces hours of rework, so let's build the one you would actually send.
facilitate: Run Write the close; give the room two minutes for both choices.
Ask one volunteer to read their two-weeks-later outcome aloud.
Point at the pattern: own words in the room, written words the same day.

expect: Next week you write what you remember
ask.respond: Exactly. The close documents the conversation while both memories still match. A week later you are writing fiction in good faith.

s3.debrief: Three lines, same day: what I heard, what I own, by when. Short enough to always send, specific enough to settle arguments.
s3.watchFor: People drafting long formal recaps. Keep it to three lines; the habit survives only while it stays cheap.
s3.transition: Quick recap, then you pick your real expectation.
s3.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the read-aloud.

facilitator.capstoneSay: Now aim it at something real. One expectation in your week that would fail the done test. Name it, roles only, pick your move and your window, and build the card. Copy it somewhere you will see it tomorrow. Two minutes, quiet, go.
facilitator.closeSay: That closes the manager standard week. Monday named the behaviors, Tuesday put the Oracle tools in your hands, and today you got the clarity moves that make expectations stick from either chair. If you want to keep pulling the thread this month, the LinkedIn Learning course New Manager Foundations with Todd Dewett is open to everyone, and the navigators are running a walk-through clinic on the standard itself. Next week the rhythm continues, and January opens the next theme, AI at Work: Start Where You Are. Go run your clarity card first.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: Someone names a real colleague while describing a fuzzy expectation
contingencies.then: Protect them warmly and immediately: 'Hold that. Roles, never names.' The moves work on any expectation; the room never needs to know whose.

contingencies.if: A learner says the written close feels passive-aggressive in their team culture
contingencies.then: Offer the friendly framing live: 'So I don't drop anything, here is what I have.' A close that reads as self-management lands well everywhere; tone is choosable.

toughQuestions.q: Won't constant clarity questions annoy busy senior people?
toughQuestions.a: Three targeted questions asked once beat a week of guessing followed by rework they have to review. Busy people benefit most from your clarity. The annoying version is vague questions asked repeatedly, which is exactly what the three-question form prevents.

toughQuestions.q: What if I restate and the other person gets impatient?
toughQuestions.a: Keep it to one sentence and frame it as a service: quick check so I build the right thing. If a ten-second restate still lands badly, that tells you something about the expectation's real clarity, and you just learned it early.

toughQuestions.q: Isn't putting things in writing a trust problem?
toughQuestions.a: The close is written to help both people, and it reads that way when it is short, same-day, and framed as keeping yourself organized. Manager Monday taught the other chair to set expectations visibly; your written close is the matching half of the same standard.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: Thursday, 45 minutes on clarity that sticks. Bring one current task or handoff that feels fuzzier than anyone has admitted. You will never be asked to name people. Live and interactive; have the session link open on your own screen.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: Did the clarity move happen? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Did you run the move on your clarity card? 2) What gap did it surface? 3) Which of the three moves is closest to becoming a reflex?
